MEDI2200 · Week 5 · DNA Replication (Parts I–III)

DNA Replication copying the genome, base by base

How a cell duplicates ~6 billion base pairs faithfully, once per division — from the antiparallel helix and its packaging, through the four steps (unwind → prime → elongate → terminate), to the three polymerases and the proofreading that keeps errors near zero. Built from Helen Rizos's three-part lecture, using its own figures.

Covers Parts I–III · §0–§10 Figures from the lecture Self-tests via the quiz

§0Orientation · learning outcomes

Copying the genome — faithfully, and exactly once

Before a cell divides, it must hand each daughter a complete, near-perfect copy of its DNA.

Every time a cell divides, both daughters need the whole instruction set — not a summary, not a slightly-corrupted version, but a faithful duplicate of all ~6 billion base pairs. DNA replication is that copying, and this lecture builds it in four steps: unwind the helix, prime each template, elongate the new strands, then terminate by tidying and sealing. Two ideas run through all of it and are worth holding from the start.

  • Semi-conservative — every new double helix ends up as one old strand + one new strand. The parent is never discarded; it is the template. (Unpacked in §3.)
  • Directionality — DNA can only be built in the 5′→3′ direction, onto a free 3′-OH. This single constraint forces almost every complication that follows, including the leading/lagging split (§6). Understand the molecule first (§1), and the machinery makes sense.
Reasoning · why fidelity is not optional

The genome is the master copy; a replication error is copied into every descendant cell. That is exactly how mutations arise. So the cell layers three safeguards — accurate base selection, polymerase proofreading (§7), and mismatch repair (§8) — to push the error rate from roughly 1 in 100,000 down toward 1 in a billion. Replication isn't just fast copying; it is copying with obsessive quality control.

Clinical / real-world

When these safeguards fail, disease follows. Inherited defects in mismatch repair cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary colorectal & endometrial cancer); loss of replication control lets cells accumulate the mutations and chromosomal chaos that define cancer. "Copy faithfully, once per division" is a rule the body enforces because breaking it is carcinogenic.

R Recall checklist — orientation
  • Semi-conservative — each daughter duplex = one parental + one new strand.
  • 5′→3′ only — DNA is always built onto a free 3′-OH; this drives everything downstream.
  • Fidelity — accurate insertion + proofreading + mismatch repair ≈ 1 error in ~10⁹.
  • Once per cycle, in S phase — errors and re-replication are carcinogenic.
§1Part I · the substrate

The molecule being copied — DNA structure

You cannot follow the machinery until you can read the molecule it works on.

DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts — a sugar, a phosphate, and a base — and the way they link gives the strand its chemistry and, crucially, its direction. As Plate 1.1 shows, the sugar-phosphate units chain together while the bases hang off to the side.

Label Key — the nucleotide & its bonds
Phosphate group
The acidic, negatively charged group on the 5′ carbon; it links one sugar to the next and makes the backbone. Why: the negative charge keeps strands apart and makes DNA water-soluble.
2′-deoxyribose
A five-carbon (pentose) sugar. Why: the "deoxy" (no 2′-OH, unlike RNA's ribose) makes DNA chemically stable — the right property for an archival master copy.
Bases
The information. Pyrimidines (thymine, cytosine) have a single carbon ring; purines (adenine, guanine) have two. Why: a one-ring base always pairs a two-ring base, keeping the helix a constant width.
Phosphodiester linkage
Joins the 3′ carbon of one nucleotide to the 5′ phosphate of the next. Why: it is what makes a strand "read" 5′→3′ — the backbone has a defined polarity.
Glycosidic bond
Joins the base to the sugar. Why: attaches the information (base) to the scaffold (sugar-phosphate).
3′-OH
The free hydroxyl on the 3′ carbon — where the next nucleotide is added. Why: this is the growing end; the whole logic of replication is "extend the 3′-OH".

Read the backbone and you read the rule that governs replication: a strand has a 5′ end (free phosphate) and a 3′ end (free hydroxyl), and new nucleotides can only be joined onto the 3′-OH. DNA therefore always grows 5′→3′. Memorise that one fact and most of the machinery becomes predictable.

§1.1The antiparallel double helix

Two strands wind together into the famous helix — but they run in opposite directions. As Plate 1.2 shows, the two sugar-phosphate backbones sit on the outside and the base pairs stack on the inside like rungs.

Label Key — helix geometry
Antiparallel strands
One runs 5′→3′, the partner 3′→5′. Why: the two 3′-OH growing ends point in opposite directions — the seed of the leading/lagging problem (§6).
Sugar-phosphate backbone (outside)
The structural rails, exposed to water. Why: keeps the reactive, information-bearing bases shielded on the inside.
Base pairs (inside)
Stacked perpendicular to the axis. A pairs T (2 H-bonds); C pairs G (3 H-bonds). Why: complementarity means each strand fully specifies the other — the physical basis of templated copying.
Reasoning · why antiparallel + complementary is the whole trick

Two properties make faithful copying possible. Complementarity (A–T, C–G) means an unwound strand is a ready-made template — read the old strand and the new one writes itself. Antiparallelism is the catch: because the strands oppose and DNA only grows 5′→3′, the two templates cannot both be copied in the simple "follow the fork" way. Hold this tension now; §6 is its resolution.

Memory hook · pairing & bond count

"C–G clings with 3, A–T holds with 2."

Three hydrogen bonds make C–G stronger and more heat-stable than A–T — GC-rich DNA is harder to melt apart. And Purine pairs Pyrimidine (two rings + one ring = constant width).

Clinical / real-world · how we know the helix

The double helix was not deduced from nothing: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction image ("Photo 51") supplied the data that revealed the helical, antiparallel structure. Watson and Crick later conceded their model "would have been most unlikely, if not impossible" without it — a standing lesson that primary experimental data underlies even the most famous models (and that credit for it was, at the time, badly misassigned).

R Recall checklist — DNA structure
  • Nucleotide = deoxyribose + phosphate + base (purine A/G, two rings; pyrimidine C/T, one ring).
  • Phosphodiester bond links 3′C→5′P; the glycosidic bond links base→sugar.
  • Strands grow only at the free 3′-OH, so DNA is always made 5′→3′.
  • Helix is antiparallel; backbone out, bases in; A–T (2 H-bonds), C–G (3 H-bonds).
§2Part I · packaging

Packaging the genome — chromosomes

Two metres of DNA per cell has to fold into a nucleus — and unfold again to be copied.

A human cell holds about two metres of DNA in a nucleus a few microns across. It manages this by condensation — winding and folding the double helix into progressively tighter chromatin, and, at cell division, into discrete chromosomes. As Plate 2.1 traces, the same molecule appears as loose "stringy" DNA, as condensed chromatin, and as the packaged chromosome.

Label Key — packaging states
'Stringy' DNA
Loosely packed chromatin. Why: this open state is what replication and transcription machinery can actually access.
Condensed DNA / chromosomes
Tightly folded for division. Why: compact chromosomes can be cleanly segregated to daughter cells without tangling or breaking.
Double-stranded DNA helix
The molecule itself, the same at every level. Why: condensation is packaging only — it changes accessibility, not the sequence.

At division each chromosome is a familiar shape (Plate 2.2): a short arm (p) and a long arm (q) meeting at the centromere, marked by reproducible light and dark bands. Those bands give every region an address.

Label Key — reading a chromosome address
p arm / q arm
Short arm = p (petit), long arm = q. Why: a locus name needs to say which arm — 9p vs 9q are different neighbourhoods.
Centromere
The constriction joining the arms; the attachment point for segregation. Why: it also defines where p ends and q begins.
Banding pattern
Reproducible light/dark stripes. Why: the bands are numbered outward from the centromere, giving each region a coordinate.
Region 9p21
Chromosome 9, p arm, band 21. Why: shows how the notation works — chromosome + arm + band.
Reasoning · why packaging is a replication problem, not just storage

Condensation and replication pull in opposite directions: DNA must be compact to be stored and segregated, but open to be copied. So chromatin is dynamically unpacked ahead of each replication fork and re-packaged behind it. The tighter a region is wound, the later it tends to replicate — which is one reason the ~30,000–50,000 origins (§4) don't all fire at once.

Clinical / real-world · why 9p21 is a famous address

The notation isn't academic — it's how clinicians name disease loci. 9p21 houses the CDKN2A tumour-suppressor genes; its deletion is one of the commonest events in melanoma and other cancers, and the region is also the strongest common-variant locus for coronary artery disease. Being able to read "9p21" is being able to place a mutation on the map.

R Recall checklist — chromosomes
  • DNA condenses: loose "stringy" chromatin ⇄ condensed chromosome; same helix throughout.
  • p = short arm, q = long arm, joined at the centromere; bands number outward.
  • Locus notation = chromosome + arm + band (e.g. 9p21).
  • Open chromatin is what the replication machinery can access.
§3Part II · the principle

Semi-conservative replication

The parent strands aren't copied and thrown away — they become half of each daughter.

Replication is semi-conservative: every new double helix consists of one original strand and one new strand joined together. As Plate 3.1 shows, the parent duplex opens, each old strand templates a new partner, and the result is two duplexes that are each half-old and half-new.

Label Key — old vs new
Old strand (template)
A parental strand, conserved intact. Why: it carries the correct sequence that specifies the new partner.
New strand
Freshly synthesised against the template. Why: pairing it base-by-base to the old strand is what makes the copy faithful.
Direction of replication
The duplex opens and copying proceeds outward from the origin. Why: foreshadows the two forks and their opposite strand logic (§4, §6).
Reasoning · why "semi-conservative" is forced by the chemistry

It could have been otherwise — the parent could have been copied and discarded (conservative), or chopped and mixed (dispersive). But complementary base-pairing makes semi-conservative the natural mechanism: the simplest way to guarantee an accurate copy is to keep each old strand and read directly off it. The old strand isn't a spare — it is the reference that keeps the new strand honest.

Memory hook

"Semi = half — half the parent survives in each child."

R Recall checklist — the principle
  • Each new duplex = one original + one new strand.
  • Each parental strand is the template for its new partner.
  • Semi-conservative is the direct consequence of complementary base-pairing.
§4Part II · Step 1

Step 1 — Unwinding & initiation

Open the helix at defined starting points, protect the exposed strands, and relieve the strain.

Before anything can be copied, the double helix must be prised open so the machinery reaches the bases. Opening happens at origins of replication — and, unlike bacteria, eukaryotes have no consensus sequence marking an origin. As Plate 4.1 shows, each fired origin opens a bubble with two replication forks that travel outward in opposite directions.

Label Key — the fork
Origin of replication
Where opening begins. Why: having defined start points lets the cell coordinate and license replication (§10) rather than start anywhere.
Replication fork
The Y-shaped junction where the strands split and new DNA is added. Why: two forks per origin means the genome is copied outward from thousands of points at once.
Bidirectional movement
The two forks travel in opposite directions. Why: halves the distance (and time) each fork must cover.

The numbers explain the strategy. Forks move at only ~2–3 kb per minute, so a single origin could never copy a whole chromosome in one S phase. Instead 30,000–50,000 origins fire per cell cycle — and not at the same time (staggered firing). The machine that opens the DNA is a licensed, loaded helicase:

  • ORC (origin recognition complex, 6 proteins) binds the origin and recruits Cdc6.
  • This loads the MCM2-7–Cdt1 complex — the replicative helicase — as a symmetrical double hexamer encircling the double-stranded DNA.
  • Cdc45 and GINS (with Pol ε) activate it; the active MCM helicase then travels along the leading strand, unwinding the two strands at each fork.
  • RPA (replication protein A) binds and coats the exposed single-stranded DNA.
  • Topoisomerases relieve the over-winding that builds up ahead of the fork.
Reasoning · why RPA and topoisomerases are non-negotiable

Unwinding creates two hazards. First, exposed single-stranded DNA is fragile and prone to snapping back or folding on itself — RPA coats it to keep it straight, protected, and available as a template. Second, unwinding a twisted helix over-winds the DNA ahead of the fork (like forcing apart a twisted rope) — topoisomerases make a transient nick, let the strain spin out, then reseal. Without them the fork would jam against its own torsion.

Reasoning · why so many origins, fired in waves

At 2–3 kb/min a lone fork would take weeks to copy one chromosome. Thousands of origins solve the throughput problem; staggering their firing spreads the demand for nucleotides and machinery across S phase and lets tightly-packed (late-replicating) regions open when their turn comes.

Clinical / real-world · topoisomerases as drug targets

Because dividing cells depend utterly on topoisomerases, blocking them is lethal to them — the basis of major chemotherapeutics. Etoposide and doxorubicin (topoisomerase II) and irinotecan/topotecan (topoisomerase I) trap the enzyme mid-cut, converting a routine nick into a permanent, cell-killing break in rapidly replicating tumour cells.

R Recall checklist — unwinding
  • Opening starts at origins (no consensus sequence in eukaryotes); each gives two bidirectional forks.
  • Forks ~2–3 kb/min; 30,000–50,000 origins fire per cycle, staggered.
  • ORC → Cdc6 → MCM2-7–Cdt1 double hexamer = the loaded helicase; Cdc45 + GINS activate it.
  • RPA coats ssDNA; topoisomerases relieve over-winding ahead of the fork.
§5Part II · Step 2

Step 2 — Priming

DNA polymerases can't start from nothing — so an RNA polymerase lays the first bricks.

Here is a genuine engineering problem: DNA polymerases can only extend an existing 3′-OH — they cannot lay down the very first nucleotide of a new strand. The cell's answer is a different enzyme that can start from scratch. As Plate 5.1 shows, once the strands are separated, primase (an RNA polymerase) synthesises a short RNA primer on each template.

Label Key — priming the fork
RNA primer (~12 nt)
A short RNA stretch complementary to the template, made 5′→3′. Why: it provides the free 3′-OH that DNA polymerase needs to begin.
Primase
An RNA polymerase that makes RNA de novo — without needing an existing 3′-OH. Why: it is the only replication enzyme that can start a strand from nothing.
Separated template strands
The unwound single strands at the fork. Why: each needs its own primer before DNA synthesis can start.

In eukaryotes primase travels as part of the DNA polymerase α–primase complex: the primase activity sits in the small p48 (Pri1) subunit, and the DNA-polymerase activity in the large p180 (Pol1) subunit. So the same complex makes the ~12-nucleotide RNA primer, then Pol α extends it with roughly 20 more nucleotides — handing off a stable primed end for the main polymerases.

Reasoning · why RNA, and why disposable

Why start with RNA rather than DNA? Because the enzyme that can initiate without a primer (an RNA polymerase) makes RNA, not DNA. The trade-off is fidelity — primase and Pol α are relatively error-prone — so the RNA primer (and Pol α's sloppy DNA) is treated as temporary scaffolding: it is later excised and replaced by high-fidelity DNA (§9). Starting fast and cleaning up afterwards beats not being able to start at all.

Memory hook

"Primase primes with RNA; polymerase can only add-on."

The only enzyme that starts from nothing is the RNA one. Everything with "DNA polymerase" in its name needs a 3′-OH handed to it first.

R Recall checklist — priming
  • DNA pols only extend a 3′-OH — they can't initiate.
  • Primase (an RNA polymerase) makes a ~12 nt RNA primer de novo, 5′→3′.
  • The Pol α–primase complex primes (p48/Pri1) then extends ~20 nt (p180/Pol1).
  • Primers are temporary — later removed and replaced by DNA (§9).
§6Part II · Step 3

Step 3 — Elongation: leading vs lagging

One template is copied smoothly; the other has to be back-stitched. Here's why.

Now the tension set up in §1 pays off. DNA synthesis extends only the 3′-OH, so both new strands are built 5′→3′ — but the two templates are antiparallel, so they point opposite ways relative to the moving fork. As Plate 6.1 shows, this splits elongation into two very different jobs.

Label Key — the two strands at the fork
Leading strand
Synthesised continuously, 5′→3′, in the same direction the fork moves. Why: its template runs the "right" way, so one primer and one long run suffice.
Lagging strand
Synthesised discontinuously, away from the fork, in short stretches. Why: its template runs the "wrong" way, so it can only be copied in backward pieces as the fork exposes more of it.
Okazaki fragments
The short (~100–200 nt) lagging-strand pieces, each with its own RNA primer. Why: they are later joined into a continuous strand (§8–§9).
3′-OH growing end
The point of addition on each new strand. Why: reinforces that everything, on both strands, is still built 5′→3′.
Reasoning · why the lagging strand must be discontinuous

The fork moves one way, but polymerase only builds 5′→3′. On the leading template that direction happens to point toward the fork, so synthesis simply follows it. On the lagging template, building 5′→3′ points away from the fork — so the polymerase can't chase the fork; it must wait for a stretch of template to be exposed, then run backward across it, over and over. The result is a series of Okazaki fragments. It isn't inefficiency — it's the only way to obey "5′→3′ only" on an antiparallel template.

Memory hook

"Leading leads (one smooth run); lagging lags (made in bits)."

R Recall checklist — elongation
  • Both strands built 5′→3′ onto a 3′-OH; needs a pre-existing primer.
  • Leading = continuous, toward the fork; lagging = discontinuous, away from the fork.
  • Okazaki fragments (~100–200 nt) build the lagging strand, each primed separately.
  • The split is forced by antiparallel templates + 5′→3′-only synthesis.
§7Part III · the enzymes

The replicative DNA polymerases (α, δ, ε)

Three related enzymes divide the labour — and the best of them check their own work.

DNA polymerases are the enzymes that actually synthesise DNA from deoxyribonucleotides, adding each new nucleotide to the growing 3′ end. They share a core toolkit and then specialise. As Plate 7.1 shows, the best ones don't just add nucleotides — they detect a mistake and reverse it.

Label Key — what a polymerase does
Template DNA
The strand being read. Why: it dictates which dNTP is correct at each position.
Addition of nucleotides
Free dNTPs added to the 3′ end. Why: extends the new strand 5′→3′, matching the template.
Incorrect base
An occasional mismatch that slips in. Why: base selection alone is only ~1-in-10⁵ accurate — not enough on its own.
3′ (→5′) exonuclease
Proofreading activity that excises the wrong terminal nucleotide, then lets synthesis resume. Why: this back-up check is what drops the error rate by 100–1000×.

The shared features are worth stating plainly: polymerases can only extend a pre-existing primer; they draw energy from hydrolysing the incoming dNTP into dNMP + pyrophosphate; they are highly processive (they synthesise long stretches without falling off); and they are generally multi-subunit. Many carry 3′ exonuclease (proofreading) activity. Eukaryotes then divide the work between three:

The three replicative DNA polymerases
PropertyPol α (priming)Pol δ (delta)Pol ε (epsilon)
FunctionRNA primer synthesis & extensionLagging-strand synthesisLeading-strand synthesis
3′ exonuclease (proofreading)NoYesYes
Fidelity (error rate)10⁻³–10⁻⁴10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶10⁻⁵–10⁻⁷
Strand displacementn.d.YesNo
ProcessivityLowLowHigh
PCNA stimulation—++++
Key interactionsMcm10, Pol δ, Ctf4PCNA, Pol αCdc45, GINS, PCNA, Ctf4
Reasoning · why proofreading matters so much

Read the fidelity column: the only difference between the sloppy Pol α (no proofreading, ~10⁻³–10⁻⁴) and the accurate Pol ε (proofreading, ~10⁻⁵–10⁻⁷) is that 3′ exonuclease. Getting the base right the first time is only ~99.99% reliable; the exonuclease that backs up over a mismatch and clips it out adds the extra 2–3 orders of magnitude. That is why Pol α's temporary DNA is later replaced (§8) and the leading/lagging strands are run by the proofreading enzymes.

Worked example · how the fidelity layers add up

Roughly how many uncorrected errors survive one replication of the diploid human genome (~6.4 × 10⁹ bp)? Layer the three safeguards.

  1. Base selection alone, error rate ≈ 10⁻⁵: 6.4×10⁹ × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 64,000 errors — far too many.
  2. Add polymerase proofreading (3′ exonuclease), error rate ≈ 10⁻⁷: 6.4×10⁹ × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 640 errors.
  3. Add mismatch repair after the fork (§8), overall ≈ 10⁻⁹: 6.4×10⁹ × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 6 errors.

Answer: ≈ 6 uncorrected errors per genome per division — three multiplied safeguards turn ~64,000 into a handful.

Clinical / real-world · when proofreading breaks

Germline mutations in the proofreading domains of POLE (Pol ε) or POLD1 (Pol δ) cause "polymerase-proofreading-associated polyposis" and a strongly raised risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer. Tumours that lose proofreading become ultra-mutated (tens of thousands of mutations) — the worked example above run in reverse. Interestingly, that heavy mutation load also makes such tumours responsive to immunotherapy.

R Recall checklist — the polymerases
  • Pols synthesise 5′→3′ from dNTPs (energy from dNTP→dNMP + PPi); only extend a primer.
  • Pol α = priming; Pol δ = lagging; Pol ε = leading.
  • 3′ exonuclease = proofreading; present in δ and ε, absent in α.
  • Fidelity & processivity rise α → δ → ε; PCNA boosts δ (+++) and ε (+).
§8Part III · the replisome

Strand synthesis in detail & the sliding clamp

Two polymerases work the two strands at once — held on by a ring that stops them falling off.

Zoom into the fork and both strands are being made simultaneously by different enzymes, coordinated in one machine. As Plate 8.1 shows, the MCM helicase (with Cdc45/GINS) leads, RPA coats the ssDNA, and Pol ε and Pol δ synthesise the leading and lagging strands respectively — each clamped to the DNA by PCNA.

Label Key — the replisome
MCM2-7 + Cdc45 + GINS
The active helicase assembly unwinding the fork. Why: sets the pace — the polymerases follow the strands it exposes.
RPA
Coats the single-stranded lagging template. Why: keeps it open and protected until Pol δ copies it.
Pol ε (leading)
Runs continuously on the leading strand. Why: its high processivity + proofreading suit one long, accurate run.
Pol δ (lagging)
Makes the Okazaki fragments. Why: restarts every ~100–200 nt, so lower processivity is acceptable — PCNA and mismatch repair make up the difference.
PCNA
The homotrimeric sliding clamp encircling the DNA. Why: tethers each polymerase so it doesn't fall off — the source of processivity.

§8.1Leading and lagging, up close

  • Pol ε — leading. Synthesises continuously and proofreads with its own 3′ exonuclease, cutting errors from ~1 in 10⁵ to ~1 in 10⁶–10⁷. It runs at ~50 nt/sec (up to ~250 nt/sec with plentiful dNTPs).
  • Pol δ — lagging. Needs a new primer every ~100–200 nt for each Okazaki fragment (RPA is displaced as it goes). On reaching the previous fragment it performs strand-displacement synthesis (lifting a flap), which FEN1 endonuclease cleaves and DNA ligase seals. Pol δ also replaces most of the low-fidelity DNA laid by Pol α.
  • Fidelity balance. Pol δ is a little less accurate than Pol ε — but that is counterbalanced by more active mismatch repair on the lagging strand.
Reasoning · why a sliding clamp exists at all

Left alone, a polymerase drifts off the DNA after only a short run — far too soon to copy a chromosome. PCNA solves this by forming a closed ring around the DNA that the polymerase grips: the enzyme can slide freely along the template but can't diffuse away. On the leading strand one clamp rides for a long run; on the lagging strand PCNA is released each time the polymerase finishes an Okazaki fragment (at its 5′ end) and reloaded for the next — which is exactly why Pol δ tolerates low intrinsic processivity.

Memory hook · ε vs δ

"ε = lEading; δ = laDding (lagging)."

And PCNA = the Proliferating Cell ring that keeps the polymerase clamped on.

Clinical / real-world · PCNA as a proliferation marker

Because PCNA is only needed where DNA is being replicated, its abundance reports how fast tissue is dividing. Pathologists use proliferation markers of exactly this kind (PCNA, Ki-67) to grade tumours — a high proliferative index means a more aggressive cancer. A molecule you learned as a "clamp" is, at the bedside, a prognostic readout.

R Recall checklist — the replisome
  • Pol ε = leading + proofreads (→ ~1 error in 10⁶–10⁷); ~50 nt/s (up to 250).
  • Pol δ = lagging; new primer every ~100–200 nt; does strand displacement → FEN1 cuts the flap → ligase seals; also replaces Pol α's DNA.
  • Lagging's lower fidelity is offset by more mismatch repair.
  • PCNA = homotrimeric sliding clamp = processivity; released at each Okazaki 5′ end.
§9Part II · Step 4

Step 4 — Termination: primer removal & ligation

Finish the job: rip out the temporary RNA, fill with DNA, and seal every nick.

The nascent lagging strand is a patchwork — DNA fragments still interrupted by the RNA primers that started each one, and by Pol α's low-fidelity DNA. Termination converts that patchwork into one continuous, all-DNA strand in three moves: remove the RNA primers, replace with DNA, and seal the nicks.

  • FEN1 endonuclease — the dominant primer-removal pathway. As Pol δ displaces the downstream fragment into a single-stranded flap, FEN1 cleaves that flap off.
  • RNase H — also contributes, removing the RNA portion of an RNA:DNA hybrid.
  • DNA chain growth then fills the gap with DNA (Pol δ), so no RNA remains.
  • DNA ligase — joins the adjacent fragments by catalysing a phosphodiester bond between the 3′-OH and the 5′-phosphate of neighbouring nucleotides, sealing the last nick.
Reasoning · why the RNA can't stay

The primers were an unavoidable compromise (§5) — but RNA has no place in the finished genome: it is chemically less stable (that 2′-OH) and was laid down by low-fidelity enzymes. So the temporary scaffolding is excised and rebuilt in accurate DNA. Ligase then makes the join covalent; until that phosphodiester bond forms, the strand is only a series of fragments resting end-to-end.

Clinical / real-world · ligase & the fork as drug targets

Sealing nicks is essential, so DNA ligase inhibitors are being explored as anticancer agents, and ligase I deficiency causes a rare immunodeficiency with growth failure. More broadly, this "finish and seal" chemistry is why fast-dividing cells are so vulnerable to drugs that jam any step of the fork — the same principle behind the topoisomerase poisons in §4.

R Recall checklist — termination
  • RNA primers are removed and replaced by DNA.
  • FEN1 cleaves the displaced ssDNA flap (dominant); RNase H also removes RNA of RNA:DNA hybrids.
  • DNA ligase seals nicks — phosphodiester bond between 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate.
§10Part III · regulation

Timing & licensing

Copy the genome in one window, and copy every base exactly once.

Replication is confined to the S phase of the cell cycle — typically about 8 hours — and tied tightly to cell-cycle control. The point of that coupling is a rule that sounds obvious but is hard to enforce across thousands of origins: DNA must be replicated once, and only once, per cycle.

Reasoning · how "exactly once" is enforced (licensing)

The trick is to split origin use into two steps that can't overlap. In G1, origins are "licensed" — ORC/Cdc6/Cdt1 load the MCM2-7 helicases (§4) — but they can't fire. In S, rising cyclin-dependent kinase activity fires the loaded helicases and simultaneously blocks any new loading. So an origin that has fired cannot be re-licensed until the cell divides and CDK falls again. Two mutually exclusive windows = each origin fires once.

Clinical / real-world · re-replication & cancer

Break the once-per-cycle rule and regions of DNA get copied twice — re-replication — producing extra copies, breaks and genome instability, a hallmark of cancer. This is also why replication licensing links back to the cell-cycle checkpoints you met with mitosis and meiosis: the cell will not enter S, or will halt within it, if the DNA or the machinery isn't ready.

R Recall checklist — timing
  • Replication occurs in S phase (~8 h).
  • Coupling to the cell cycle enforces replicate once per cycle.
  • Licensing: MCM helicases loaded in G1, fired in S; no re-loading after firing.
  • Re-replication → genome instability → cancer.
